title: Hands-on Exercise 1B
text:
This exercise builds a choropleth workflow for Singapore’s 2024 resident population. I prepare demographic indicators at subzone level, join them to the Master Plan 2019 boundaries, and compare mapping choices rather than accepting the first default map.






NoteData note



The current official boundary download is GeoJSON and already exposes its attributes as columns. The original lesson’s rvest step was needed to unpack an HTML description stored inside an older KML file. I checked the new file and did not parse HTML that is no longer present. This keeps the workflow faithful to the task while avoiding an artificial cleaning step.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B
text:
1. Setup and import
The download script saves the official boundary and unpacks the SingStat ZIP. I explicitly exclude the separate notes CSV when selecting the data table.

population_files <- list.files(
  file.path(data_dir, "singstat-population-2024"),
  pattern = "[.]csv$",
  recursive = TRUE,
  full.names = TRUE
)

population_file <- population_files[
  !startsWith(basename(population_files), "Notes_")
][1]

basename(population_file)

[1] "respopagesextod2024.csv"



mpsz2019 <- st_read(
  file.path(data_dir, "mp19-subzone.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  st_make_valid() |>
  st_transform(3414)

population_raw <- read_csv(population_file, show_col_types = FALSE)

tibble(
  dataset = c("MP2019 subzones", "Population records"),
  rows = c(nrow(mpsz2019), nrow(population_raw)),
  columns = c(ncol(mpsz2019), ncol(population_raw))
)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  dataset              rows columns
  <chr>               <int>   <int>
1 MP2019 subzones       332      14
2 Population records 100928       7



glimpse(population_raw)

1      676         12  DEPOT ROAD    BMSZ12      N BUKIT MERAH         BM

Inspecting the files first caught an important detail: population is split by age group, sex and dwelling type. A simple sum of the raw rows is valid only after grouping by geography and age; otherwise it is easy to lose track of what each number represents.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B
text:
2. Preparing demographic variables
I use the lesson’s three life-stage groups: 0–19 as young residents, 20–64 as economically active, and 65 or older as aged residents. The dependency ratio is the combined young and aged population per 100 economically active residents.

young_groups <- c("0_to_4", "5_to_9", "10_to_14", "15_to_19")

working_groups <- c(
  "20_to_24", "25_to_29", "30_to_34", "35_to_39", "40_to_44",
  "45_to_49", "50_to_54", "55_to_59", "60_to_64"
)

aged_groups <- c(
  "65_to_69", "70_to_74", "75_to_79", "80_to_84",
  "85_to_89", "90_and_over"
)


population2024 <- population_raw |>
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) |>
  summarise(Pop = sum(Pop, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(PA, SZ) |>
  summarise(
    YOUNG = sum(Pop[AG %in% young_groups]),
    ECONOMY_ACTIVE = sum(Pop[AG %in% working_groups]),
    AGED = sum(Pop[AG %in% aged_groups]),
    TOTAL = sum(Pop),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    DEPENDENCY = if_else(
      ECONOMY_ACTIVE > 0,
      100 * (YOUNG + AGED) / ECONOMY_ACTIVE,
      NA_real_
    ),
    PA_KEY = str_to_upper(str_squish(PA)),
    SZ_KEY = str_to_upper(str_squish(SZ))
  )

population2024 |>
  arrange(desc(TOTAL)) |>
  select(PA, SZ, YOUNG, ECONOMY_ACTIVE, AGED, TOTAL, DEPENDENCY) |>
  slice_head(n = 8)

The raw counts are rounded to the nearest ten by SingStat. I therefore avoid presenting false precision, especially when comparing small subzones.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B
text:
3. Joining attributes to geometry
The two datasets use different capitalization, so I create upper-case, trimmed keys for planning area and subzone before joining. Using both keys is safer than subzone name alone.

mpsz_pop2024 <- mpsz2019 |>
  mutate(
    PA_KEY = str_to_upper(str_squish(PLN_AREA_N)),
    SZ_KEY = str_to_upper(str_squish(SUBZONE_N))
  ) |>
  left_join(population2024, by = c("PA_KEY", "SZ_KEY"))

join_check <- tibble(
  check = c("Boundary features", "Features with population", "Features without population"),
  value = c(
    nrow(mpsz_pop2024),
    sum(!is.na(mpsz_pop2024$TOTAL)),
    sum(is.na(mpsz_pop2024$TOTAL))
  )
)

join_check

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  check                       value
  <chr>                       <int>
1 Boundary features             332
2 Features with population      332
3 Features without population     0


Some planning subzones have no resident record. I keep them as NA rather than changing them to zero: “no matched record” and “confirmed zero residents” are not the same statement.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B
text:
4. A first choropleth
qtm() gives me a fast diagnostic map. It is useful for checking the join and spatial pattern before spending time on design.

tmap_mode("plot")
qtm(
  mpsz_pop2024,
  fill = "TOTAL",
  fill.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = "brewer.blues"),
  fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Residents")
)




Quick choropleth of total resident population in 2024.




The pattern is plausible, but a continuous colour ramp hides the decisions behind class boundaries. I next compare two explicit classification methods.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B
text:
5. Comparing classification methods
Quantiles place roughly the same number of subzones in each class. Equal intervals preserve equal numeric widths, but a few high-population subzones can leave most areas crowded into the lower classes.

map_quantile <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "brewer.blues"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependants per 100")
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.4) +
  tm_title("Quantile")

map_equal <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "equal", n = 5, values = "brewer.blues"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependants per 100")
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.4) +
  tm_title("Equal interval")

tmap_arrange(map_quantile, map_equal, ncol = 2)




Dependency ratio classified with quantiles and equal intervals.




For a national comparison I prefer quantiles because differences across the full distribution remain visible. Equal intervals would be preferable if the numeric distance between classes were the main message.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B
text:
6. Refined map design
I keep one sequential palette because dependency ratio has a natural low-to- high order. A thin white boundary separates adjacent subzones without overpowering the fill, and the compass and scale bar make the map usable beyond the immediate classroom context.

dependency_breaks <- quantile(
  mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY,
  probs = seq(0, 1, length.out = 6),
  na.rm = TRUE
) |>
  as.numeric() |>
  unique()

refined_map <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      breaks = dependency_breaks,
      values = "brewer.blues"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependants per 100\nworking-age residents")
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.35) +
  tm_title("Resident dependency ratio, 2024") +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", position = tm_pos_in("left", "top")) +
  tm_scalebar(position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom")) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)

refined_map




Refined dependency-ratio choropleth for Singapore subzones.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B
text:
7. Small multiples
The same colour scale should not be forced onto groups with very different totals. I therefore create two maps with their own quantile breaks and arrange them side by side.

map_young <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "YOUNG",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "brewer.greens"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Age 0–19")
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.3) +
  tm_title("Young residents")

map_aged <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "AGED",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "brewer.purples"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Age 65+")
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "white", lwd = 0.3) +
  tm_title("Aged residents")

tmap_arrange(map_young, map_aged, ncol = 2)




Young and aged residents shown as coordinated small multiples.




Reading the maps together shows that “many older residents” is not simply the opposite of “many young residents”. Several established housing areas have large totals in both groups, so the dependency ratio remains valuable as a relative measure.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B
text:
8. Selection and a complementary chart
I define a transparent selection rule: the top 10% of populated subzones by dependency ratio. The map locates them, while the bar chart makes the ranking and values easier to compare.

dependency_cutoff <- quantile(
  mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY,
  0.90,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

high_dependency <- mpsz_pop2024 |>
  filter(!is.na(DEPENDENCY), DEPENDENCY >= dependency_cutoff)

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "#edf1f5", col = "white", lwd = 0.25) +
  tm_shape(high_dependency) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "#6f82aa", col = "#465d91", lwd = 0.7) +
  tm_title("Top 10% by dependency ratio")









high_dependency |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(DEPENDENCY) |>
  slice_tail(n = 12) |>
  mutate(SUBZONE_N = fct_reorder(SUBZONE_N, DEPENDENCY)) |>
  ggplot(aes(DEPENDENCY, SUBZONE_N)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#6f82aa") +
  labs(
    x = "Dependants per 100 working-age residents",
    y = NULL,
    title = "Subzones with the highest dependency ratios"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()




Highest dependency ratios among Singapore subzones.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B
text:
9. Interactive exploration
The static map communicates one main pattern; the interactive version supports lookup. Hovering or clicking lets a reader inspect the subzone name, planning area and demographic values without printing labels over the whole island.

tmap_mode("view")

tm_shape(st_transform(mpsz_pop2024, 4326)) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "DEPENDENCY",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "brewer.blues"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Dependency ratio"),
    popup.vars = c(
      "Subzone" = "SUBZONE_N",
      "Planning area" = "PLN_AREA_N",
      "Total residents" = "TOTAL",
      "Young residents" = "YOUNG",
      "Aged residents" = "AGED",
      "Dependency ratio" = "DEPENDENCY"
    )
  )





tmap_mode("plot")

title: Hands-on Exercise 1B
text:
10. What I learned
The join deserves as much attention as the map. Normalising both geographic keys and retaining unmatched boundaries prevents silent data loss. I also found that classification is an analytical decision: quantiles reveal relative position, while equal intervals preserve numeric distance. Finally, pairing a choropleth with a ranking chart makes the result easier to interpret than either view alone.

ISSS626 Geospatial Analytics and Applications.
by Zhenhua Liu

title: Hands-on Exercise 1A
text:
This exercise is my first end-to-end spatial workflow in R. I import polygon, line and point data, put every layer in a common projected coordinate reference system, and then use spatial relationships to answer two practical questions: how much land is covered by a cycling-path buffer in Tampines West, and how pre-school provision varies between subzones.






NoteData note



The lesson was originally written around KML and shapefile downloads. The current official portals provide GeoJSON, so I kept the analytical intention but used the live formats available in September 2026. Raw files are obtained by R/download-data.R and are not duplicated in the Git repository.

text:
This exercise is my first end-to-end spatial workflow in R. I import polygon, line and point data, put every layer in a common projected coordinate reference system, and then use spatial relationships to answer two practical questions: how much land is covered by a cycling-path buffer in Tampines West, and how pre-school provision varies between subzones.






NoteData note



The lesson was originally written around KML and shapefile downloads. The current official portals provide GeoJSON, so I kept the analytical intention but used the live formats available in September 2026. Raw files are obtained by R/download-data.R and are not duplicated in the Git repository.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1A
text:
1. Setup and data import
I first read one example of each geometry type. Looking at the geometry column separately from the attribute table helped me remember that an sf object is still a data frame; it simply carries a special list-column for shapes.

mpsz <- st_read(file.path(data_dir, "mp14-subzone.geojson"), quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_make_valid()

preschool <- st_read(file.path(data_dir, "preschools.geojson"), quiet = TRUE)
cycling <- st_read(file.path(data_dir, "cycling-paths.geojson"), quiet = TRUE)

tibble(
  layer = c("Subzones", "Pre-schools", "Cycling paths"),
  features = c(nrow(mpsz), nrow(preschool), nrow(cycling)),
  geometry = c(
    as.character(unique(st_geometry_type(mpsz))[1]),
    as.character(unique(st_geometry_type(preschool))[1]),
    as.character(unique(st_geometry_type(cycling))[1])
  ),
  crs = c(st_crs(mpsz)$input, st_crs(preschool)$input, st_crs(cycling)$input)
)

title: Hands-on Exercise 1A
text:
2. Coordinate reference systems
The imported files describe the same country but do not necessarily use the same CRS. Latitude/longitude is suitable for storage and web display; distance and area calculations need a projected CRS. I therefore transform every layer to SVY21 / Singapore TM (EPSG:3414).

crs_before <- tibble(
  layer = c("Subzones", "Pre-schools", "Cycling paths"),
  epsg = c(st_crs(mpsz)$epsg, st_crs(preschool)$epsg, st_crs(cycling)$epsg)
)

mpsz <- st_transform(mpsz, 3414)
preschool <- st_transform(preschool, 3414)
cycling <- st_transform(cycling, 3414)

crs_before

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  layer          epsg
  <chr>         <int>
1 Subzones       4326
2 Pre-schools    4326
3 Cycling paths  4326








TipMy check before analysis



st_set_crs() only changes the coordinate label. It does not move the geometry. Because these layers already have valid coordinates, st_transform() is the correct operation.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1A
section: 3. Converting Airbnb records to spatial points
text:
3. Converting Airbnb records to spatial points
The Airbnb file is an ordinary CSV. Its longitude and latitude columns become point geometry in WGS 84, after which I transform the points to EPSG:3414 for a valid overlay with the planning boundaries.

airbnb_raw <- read_csv(
  file.path(data_dir, "airbnb-listings.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

airbnb <- airbnb_raw |>
  filter(!is.na(longitude), !is.na(latitude)) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(3414)

title: Hands-on Exercise 1A
text:
4. Five-metre cycling-path buffer
I select Tampines West, intersect the cycling lines with its boundary, and buffer the remaining lines by five metres. Summing every buffer polygon can double-count overlaps, so I dissolve them before calculating the final area.

tampines_west <- mpsz |>
  filter(SUBZONE_N == "TAMPINES WEST")

cycling_in_tampines <- st_intersection(cycling, tampines_west)
cycling_buffer <- st_buffer(cycling_in_tampines, dist = 5)
cycling_buffer_union <- st_union(cycling_buffer)

buffer_result <- tibble(
  measure = c("Sum before dissolving", "Dissolved footprint"),
  area_m2 = c(
    sum(as.numeric(st_area(cycling_buffer))),
    as.numeric(st_area(cycling_buffer_union))
  )
) |>
  mutate(area_km2 = area_m2 / 1e6)

buffer_result

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  measure               area_m2 area_km2
  <chr>                   <dbl>    <dbl>
1 Sum before dissolving 119204.    0.119
2 Dissolved footprint   106423.    0.106



ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = tampines_west, fill = "#eef3f8", colour = "#465d91") +
  geom_sf(data = cycling_buffer_union, fill = "#73c6b6", colour = NA, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_sf(data = cycling_in_tampines, colour = "#24435d", linewidth = 0.35) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(title = "Cycling-path buffer", subtitle = "Tampines West, 5 metres") +
  theme_void()




Dissolved five-metre buffer around cycling paths in Tampines West.




The dissolved result is the more defensible estimate of land covered. The gap between the two numbers is a useful reminder that geometry overlaps are not just a display issue—they change summary statistics.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1A
text:
5. Pre-school count and density
st_intersects() returns the pre-schools falling inside each subzone. I keep both the count and the density because they answer different questions: count describes total provision, while density adjusts for the physical size of the subzone.

mpsz_summary <- mpsz |>
  mutate(
    preschool_count = lengths(st_intersects(mpsz, preschool)),
    area_km2 = as.numeric(st_area(geometry)) / 1e6,
    preschool_density = preschool_count / area_km2
  )

highest_count <- mpsz_summary |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  slice_max(preschool_count, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  select(SUBZONE_N, PLN_AREA_N, preschool_count, area_km2, preschool_density)

highest_count

       SUBZONE_N PLN_AREA_N preschool_count area_km2 preschool_density
1  TAMPINES EAST   TAMPINES              72 4.339828          16.59052
2 WOODLANDS EAST  WOODLANDS              54 2.553464          21.14775
3       ALJUNIED    GEYLANG              40 2.959367          13.51640
4  TAMPINES WEST   TAMPINES              38 3.475208          10.93460
5    BEDOK NORTH      BEDOK              38 3.203660          11.86143



ggplot(mpsz_summary) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = preschool_count), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.12) +
  geom_sf(data = preschool, colour = "#34495e", alpha = 0.45, size = 0.22) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", direction = -1) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(title = "Pre-schools by subzone", fill = "Count") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())




Pre-school locations and subzone-level counts.





density_data <- mpsz_summary |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(is.finite(preschool_density))

p_hist <- ggplot(density_data, aes(preschool_density)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "#6f82aa", colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Pre-schools per km²", y = "Subzones", title = "Density distribution") +
  theme_minimal()

p_scatter <- ggplot(
  density_data,
  aes(preschool_count, preschool_density)
) +
  geom_point(colour = "#465d91", alpha = 0.65) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "#d45b5b", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Pre-school count", y = "Pre-schools per km²", title = "Count versus density") +
  theme_minimal()

gridExtra::grid.arrange(p_hist, p_scatter, ncol = 2)




Distribution of density and the relationship between count and density.




The scatterplot confirms that a high count does not automatically imply the highest density. Small subzones can rank highly after area is taken into account. If I were extending this analysis, I would next relate provision to the number of young children rather than land area alone.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1A
text:
6. What I learned
Three checks made the workflow more reliable: inspect geometry and attributes before analysis, transform rather than relabel a valid CRS, and dissolve overlapping buffers before measuring area. The exercise also showed me why a map and a statistical plot should be read together—the map reveals geography, while the histogram and scatterplot reveal the shape of the values.
